The number went up seven times. The stone count did not move at all, and that is the part to read twice.

Vietnamese investigators now put the smuggling network at $73 million of diamonds moved into the country, with about $57 million of stones identified and more than 30 people arrested or detained. This desk filed the case on July 16 at 280 billion dong, roughly $10.65 million, which was the figure in the charge sheet at the time. That number described the prosecution. The $73 million describes the pipeline.

The mechanism cost nothing and left no record. Couriers flew from Hong Kong into Vietnamese airports with stones in luggage, shoes and clothing, orders arranged over WhatsApp, and released the goods only to a recipient holding a bank note whose eleven-character serial number matched one agreed in advance. There is no ledger to subpoena, no wallet to trace, and no message that has to name a stone.

The stones did not stay in a back room. Saigon Jewelry Company, the state-owned retailer that sets Vietnam's benchmark gold price, bought more than 3,400 of them for about $19 million, at roughly a third below market. The former director of P-Lab, which handles about 70% of Vietnamese certification, is among those charged, with smuggled stones allegedly re-papered under the lab's own certificates.

Twenty-eight thousand stones crossed a border 141 times over two years and were absorbed by named retailers. The failure was not at the airport. It was at the counter.

The weakest jewellery quarter of the modern gold era belongs to China, and the value line hid it.

Mainland Chinese gold jewellery demand fell to 50.0 tonnes in the second quarter, down 28% from 69.2 tonnes a year earlier and the lowest second quarter since 2004, per the World Gold Council's Gold Demand Trends published July 30. Across the half the country took 136 tonnes, down 30%. The council called the global quarter one of the weakest in its data series, and China is where most of that weakness sits.

Measured in money, the same half-year was worth about $21 billion, up 11%. Consumers in the largest gold jewellery market on earth bought roughly 30% less metal and paid roughly 11% more for it. For a manufacturer that is not a demand collapse but a change in what is being sold: fewer grams, lighter pieces, more labour content per sale.

The rest of the map fell in the same direction. India took 75.1 tonnes, down 15%. The Middle East fell 19% to 32.2 tonnes. The United States fell 25% to 22.2 tonnes, the sharpest percentage decline among the major markets and the one nobody has quoted, in a summer spent describing American demand as the strong lane. Global fabrication came to 278.2 tonnes against 335.3.

Value figures rise mechanically with the metal and will keep printing records while gold holds above $4,000. Price your inventory in grams and read the press releases in dollars.

The theft numbers improved and the loss numbers did not. That is the whole of the 2026 retail crime picture.

The National Retail Federation's Impact of Retail Theft and Violence study, published in late July, found shoplifting incidents down 12.4% in 2025 and merchandise theft down 8.1%. Against that, 69% of retailers reported rising phone scams, 42% reported growth in gift-card theft and fraud, 40% named organised retail crime, and half reported more repeat offenders. Jewellery, gold and watches rank among the categories generating the highest dollar losses to organised groups.

The jewellery series says it in harder numbers. The Jewelers' Security Alliance counted 1,233 crimes against United States jewellery firms in 2025, down 13% from 1,420, on total losses that rose to $144.7 million from $142.5 million. Fewer incidents, each one more expensive.

The violence line is the one that should change behaviour. Robberies involving guns, mace or vehicles rose to 27% of the total from 17%. Incidents involving mace went from 3 to 14. Vehicles driven into stores went from none reported to 13. Crimes at jewellers' own homes rose from 4 to 11. Two people in the trade died in 2025, against four the year before.

A declining headline is the dangerous part of this data set. The exposure has moved off the display case and onto the phone, the gift card and the shipment, where nothing appears on a camera and a loss is written off as bad debt rather than logged as a crime. Two deaths is a better year than four and is not a good year.
